title: Solicitor entry: Diverse routes yield unequal attainment
desc: Separates access from examination outcomes, identifying apprenticeships as promising while leaving causes of pass-rate disparities unresolved.

kps.k: Diverse entry to solicitor qualification does not imply equal attainment.
kps.d: The SRA's four-year SQE review frames the central issue as broad participation alongside uneven outcomes. Its internationally drawn cohort is more ethnically diverse than the UK population and solicitor profession; around 37% of candidates come from less privileged backgrounds. Yet White candidates have higher overall pass rates, and less privileged candidates generally perform worse. These comparisons describe participation and attainment, not proof that the SQE itself causes or removes inequality.

qs.q: ## The ethnic make-up of SQE entry cohorts is diverse  The SQE entry cohort, which includes candidates living in the UK and in other countries, is more ethnically diverse than the UK population, when compared with the 2021 census data.
qs.a: The SQE four years on – facts and figures · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: It is also more diverse than the solicitor profession.
qs.a: The SQE four years on – facts and figures · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Measured associations explain only part of attainment differences and do not settle their causes.
kps.d: Kaplan's analysis associates university ranking and degree classification with roughly 22–23% of SQE1 score variance; SQE1 performance and university ranking explain about 30% of SQE2 variance. Ethnicity alone accounts for reported shares of 7.6% and 4.2%, respectively—score-variance estimates, not pass-rate gaps. After adjustment, parental education and household-earner occupation explain only 0.3% and 0.1% of SQE1 variance. The SRA reports 67% unexplained variance and proposes motivation, aptitude and study time as possible explanations, not measured findings. Its cited Exeter research describes multiple, complex causes of ethnic attainment differences.

qs.q: This multivariate analysis shows that the rank of the university attended by a candidate and their degree classification together explain about 22% of the variance in candidates' SQE1 scores - 11.9% for university rank and 10.6% for degree classification.
qs.a: The SQE four years on – facts and figures · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: For SQE2 candidates, SQE1 performance and university ranking explain about 30% of the variance.
qs.a: The SQE four years on – facts and figures · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Apprenticeships provide the SRA's clearest positive evidence for an inclusive qualification route.
kps.d: More than 800 solicitor apprentices had passed the SQE, and apprentices were more likely than the overall cohort to come from less privileged backgrounds. Their reported pass rates were around 71% for SQE1 and 93% for SQE2, against 66% and 85% overall. School-leaver and graduate apprentices performed similarly. The SRA interprets these results as support for social mobility through combined work and study; the comparisons do not isolate whether the training model, selection or other factors explain their performance.

qs.q: More than 800 apprentices have passed SQE, with the data showing these candidates are more likely to come from less privileged socio-economic backgrounds than SQE candidates as a whole.
qs.a: The SQE four years on – facts and figures · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: The overall solicitor apprentice pass rates have been around 71% for SQE1 and 93% for SQE2, compared with 66% and 85% for the whole cohort.
qs.a: The SQE four years on – facts and figures · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Disability findings offer qualified reassurance rather than a universal answer to concerns about fairness.
kps.d: The SRA reports that candidates declaring a disability perform at least as well as other SQE candidates, unlike under the LPC. In response to concerns about neurodivergent disadvantage, it cites Kaplan's September 2024–July 2025 analysis showing slightly higher scores and pass rates among first-time candidates with reasonable adjustments for disclosed neurodivergent conditions. The reassurance applies directly to that studied population, not all neurodivergent candidates. The supplied material records concerns through the SRA's account rather than presenting a separate opposing analysis.

qs.q: The data also shows that candidates who declare a disability perform at least as well as other candidates on the SQE.
qs.a: The SQE four years on – facts and figures · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: This is not the case with the previous qualification route – the Legal Practice Course (LPC).
qs.a: The SQE four years on – facts and figures · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Pass-rate variation and weaker outcomes for some routes make preparation a practical concern.
kps.d: Across November 2021–July 2025, first-time pass rates ranged from 46–60% for SQE1 and 69–84% for SQE2. The SRA attributes variation to cohort performance rather than changing standards. It reports that around 20% of SQE1 resitters pass, while previously qualified lawyers and candidates whose first language is not English generally have lower pass rates. LPC graduates also fare worse on SQE2. The SRA cautions them against relying on LPC studies alone and suggests that testing readiness to practise, rather than readiness to start a training contract, may explain the difference.

qs.q: It covers eight SQE1 and 12 SQE2 assessments taken between November 2021 and July 2025, and more than 30,000 candidates assessed in 50 countries.
qs.a: The SQE four years on – facts and figures · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: The pass rates for candidates sitting SQE1 for the first time have ranged from 46% to 60%.
qs.a: The SQE four years on – facts and figures · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: The consumer-survey extract cannot establish a broader link between demographic diversity and legal-service choice.
kps.d: Tracker Survey 2025 supplies an ethnicity table but no column headings identifying populations or periods. Its last percentage column records 65% White British and 32% ethnic minority, but neither those figures nor the signed differences support reliable trend claims. The extract therefore supplies no interpretable evidence about consumer choice, qualification outcomes or a connection between them.

vlens.an: Within this curated set of regulators, courts and professional bodies, the substantive SRA evidence supports the proposition that broad access to solicitor qualification coexists with unequal attainment. The SRA distinguishes cohort diversity from examination outcomes, reports ethnic and socio-economic performance differences, and treats their causes as complex and only partly explained by measured variables. It also supports the proposition’s qualified optimism about apprenticeships: apprentices are more likely to come from less privileged backgrounds and have higher reported pass rates than the overall cohort. Material internal variation arises because the consumer-survey extract does not address qualification routes or attainment and lacks headings needed to interpret its ethnicity table; it is therefore uninformative rather than contrary. Further qualification comes from the SRA’s disability and neurodivergence findings, which are reassuring for the specific populations studied but do not negate disparities elsewhere or establish universal fairness.

qs.q: The overall solicitor apprentice pass rates have been around 71% for SQE1 and 93% for SQE2, compared with 66% and 85% for the whole cohort.
qs.a: The SQE four years on – facts and figures · Regulators & courts · 2026

elens.an: The 2025 consumer-tracker extract neither supports nor challenges the proposition that diverse solicitor-entry routes coexist with unequal attainment and that apprenticeships are promising. It reports ethnicity percentages, but missing column headings leave the populations, periods and meaning of the signed changes uncertain. More importantly, it provides no evidence about SQE participation, pass rates, apprenticeships or the causes of attainment disparities. With only this source in the facet, there is no meaningful internal variation to assess; its role is limited to reinforcing the synthesis’s caution that these consumer-survey data cannot establish claims about qualification access or outcomes.

The sole curated 2026 source supports the proposition that broader access to solicitor qualification coexists with unequal attainment. The SRA reports an ethnically and socio-economically diverse SQE cohort but materially different outcomes by ethnicity, socio-economic background, sex and prior academic attainment. It also supports the proposition’s caution on causation: measured variables explain only part of score variation, while the cited research characterises ethnic attainment differences as arising from multiple complex factors. Its strongest positive evidence concerns apprenticeships, whose candidates are more likely to come from less privileged backgrounds and have higher reported pass rates than the overall cohort. Material variation prevents a uniformly negative account: candidates declaring disabilities perform at least as well as others, adjusted neurodivergent candidates perform slightly better in the studied population, and sex differences reverse between SQE1 and SQE2. Conversely, resitters, previously qualified lawyers, LPC graduates and candidates whose first language is not English have weaker reported outcomes. These findings reinforce the need to separate access, attainment and preparation, without establishing that the SQE itself causes the disparities or that apprenticeships alone cause better results. Because this facet contains one curated source, its position should not be treated as representative of all current-wave views.
